title: Samgyetang
subtitle: Ginseng and garlic whole chicken soup
excerpt: Samgyetang is a Korean restorative soup of a whole small chicken stuffed with glutinous rice and simmered with garlic and ginger until the meat is falling from the bone. It serves 2 and takes about 105 minutes. Ginseng root is the traditional addition and adds a bitter, earthy note to the broth.
sourceNotes: Samgyetang is one of Korea's most culturally significant dishes, eaten on the three hottest days of the lunar calendar known as Sambok. The tradition of eating warming, fortifying food in summer to restore energy lost through heat and perspiration has been documented in Korean records for over a thousand years. The dish was historically associated with royalty and later became available to all.

glossaryTerms.definition: Samgyetang breaks into three parts: sam (ginseng), gye (chicken), and tang (soup). The name describes the dish directly. It is the definitive Korean summer tonic soup, eaten on the hottest days of the year as a restorative meal believed to replenish vital energy lost through heat and sweating.

Sambok refers to the three hottest days of the Korean lunar calendar: Chobok, Jungbok, and Malbok, which fall across July and August. Eating samgyetang on these days is a long-standing Korean tradition. The belief is that consuming a hot, nourishing meal on the hottest days of summer helps the body regain strength.

content.text: This recipe serves 2, with one whole small chicken per bowl, and takes about 105 minutes.

is the Korean dish of a whole small chicken stuffed with glutinous rice, garlic, and ginger, then simmered in water until the broth is milky and the meat is completely tender. It is eaten on the three hottest days of summer, known as

Use the smallest whole chickens you can find, around 800g each, ideally poussin or small spring chickens. Rinse the rice but do not soak it before stuffing: dry rice absorbs the chicken juices as it cooks and thickens the cavity filling beautifully. Tie the legs together with kitchen twine after stuffing to hold the filling in place. Add the optional ginseng root to the pot if you have it. It contributes a slightly bitter, medicinal note that is part of the dish's character.
Rinse each chicken inside and out under cold water. Pat dry.

Divide the rinsed rice between the two chicken cavities. Push 2 garlic cloves and a few slices of ginger into each cavity on top of the rice. The rice should fill the cavity about two-thirds full to leave room for expansion.
Tie the legs of each chicken together with kitchen twine to seal the cavity opening.
Place both chickens in a large pot. Add the remaining 6 garlic cloves, the ginseng root if using, and 2 litres of cold water.
Bring to the boil, skimming off any foam. Reduce the heat to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 80 to 90 minutes until the chicken is completely tender and the broth is milky white.
Carefully lift each chicken into a deep bowl. Ladle the broth over and around. Drizzle with sesame oil and scatter the spring onions over the top. Season with salt and white pepper at the table.

items.symptom: The rice has pushed out of the cavity
items.cause: Too much rice was used or the legs were not tied tightly enough
items.fix: Use no more than 40g of rice per bird and tie the legs firmly. The rice will still cook in the broth if it escapes and the flavour is unchanged

items.symptom: The broth is very pale and thin
items.cause: The simmer was too gentle or the cooking time was too short
items.fix: Turn up the heat slightly to a moderate simmer and continue cooking for another 20 minutes. The broth deepens and whitens as collagen releases from the bones

items.symptom: The chicken skin is falling off and breaking up
items.cause: The chicken was too large or cooked at too high a boil
items.fix: Use small birds and keep the simmer very gentle. The skin will still be delicate but should hold its shape if the chicken is lifted carefully with two spoons

content.text: Samgyetang is served one whole chicken per person, in a large stone bowl or deep ceramic pot. It is eaten slowly, with salt and white pepper for seasoning added at the table. The rice inside the chicken is scooped out and eaten alongside the meat. The broth is drunk throughout the meal. Samgyetang restaurants in Seoul are famous for their queues on Sambok days, with customers waiting an hour or more to eat this one dish. At home, it is a weekend project that rewards patient simmering with one of the most satisfying soups in Korean cooking.
